title: Why was it made, and what was going on?

---
order: 3
unit: purpose
title: Why was it made, and what was going on?
node: AC9HH7S03 n2
summary: "Context asks what was going on when a source was made: not just the place, but the particular events and conditions around it. Purpose asks why it was made: to show power, to run a state, to honour someone, to record what happened. Two mistakes are common. 'Ancient China' is a setting, not a context. And 'it shows the emperor' is content, not purpose. Context and purpose together explain what a source includes and what it leaves out."
language: maths
hook: "The First Emperor had words cut into stone on mountains. Why would a ruler do that? What was going on that made it worth the trouble?"
---
Once you know **who** made a source and **what** it shows, two more questions help you read it.

**Context** is what was going on around the source when it was made. It is the particular events and conditions of the time, not just the place or the period. "Ancient China" is a place and a time, but it is not a context.

**Purpose** is **why** it was made. What was it for? What did the maker want people to do, think or remember?

For ancient sources, the maker rarely tells us the purpose. No Qin text says why the clay army was made, for example. Historians work out a likely purpose from the source, its context and other evidence, so purposes are often said with "probably" or "historians think".

Here is a source from the last lesson, with its context filled in.

> **Source C: an inscription.** Words cut into stone, set up on a mountain by order of the First Emperor on one of his tours, around 219 BCE. It praises the emperor as a ruler without equal. It says he brought peace and order, that everyone now lives in peace, and that everyone lives under one set of laws, weights and measures. *Context:* a few years earlier the Qin had defeated six rival kingdoms and joined them into one empire. Many people in the new empire had been enemies of the Qin.

## Predict: a better context

```step
stage: predict
insight: "Committing first shows whether students reach for a setting ('ancient China') or a specific circumstance."
check:
  type: predict
  q: "Which is the best description of the context of the inscription in Source C?"
  options: ["The Qin had just joined six rival kingdoms into one", "It was made in ancient China, in Qin times", "It was carved into stone on a mountain", "It praises the emperor as a ruler without equal"]
  actual: "The Qin had just joined six rival kingdoms into one empire. That is what was going on. 'Ancient China, in Qin times' is only the setting, stone on a mountain is how and where it was made, and the praise is what it says."
```

## Try: match the purpose

```step
stage: run
insight: "Matching a source to what it was for shows that different sources of the same time have different jobs."
check:
  type: match
  q: "Each of these sources was made for a different reason. Match each source to its most likely purpose (for the ancient ones, this is what historians think)."
  pairs:
    - ["Source A: a clay warrior in the emperor's tomb", "Probably to guard and serve the emperor after his death"]
    - ["Source B: laws on bamboo slips", "To tell officials which rules to follow"]
    - ["Source C: a stone inscription on a mountain", "Probably to show his power and win people's support"]
    - ["Source D: a museum label", "To explain the warriors to visitors"]
```

Was your guess right? Notice that each source had a different job, even though three of them were made for the same ruler.

## Practise: what the card tells you

Label each sentence of Source C's card. Think carefully before you use every label.

```step
stage: practise
insight: "Labelling the card shows that it states its origin, content and context, but not its purpose: purpose is worked out from the others."
try: { playground: board, starter: "text.yml#run", height: 420 }
hint: ["Context is what was going on around the source, not what the source says.", "Does any sentence say why the stone was made? Or only what it says?"]

The card tells you what it says (content) and what was going on (context). Purpose is something historians work out from those, which is why it is said with 'probably'." }
```

## Vary: another source

```step
stage: modify
insight: "Applying both questions to a new source, and noticing how purpose changes who the source is for."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Source B is a set of Qin laws on bamboo slips. Which is the best context?"
      options: ["The Qin were running a big state and needed officials everywhere to follow the same rules", "It was the Qin period in ancient China, more than 2000 years ago", "The slips were buried with an official in a tomb at Shuihudi", "The slips list rules for grain stores and punishments"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "That is only the setting: a place and a time.", "That is where they were found. It says nothing about what was going on when they were written.", "That is what the slips say, which is content."]
      explain: "The Qin ran a large empire with many officials. Writing the rules down meant officials everywhere could follow the same ones."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Who were the bamboo slips mainly written for?"
      options: ["Officials who had to follow the rules", "Everyone in the empire, to admire the emperor", "Farmers, so they knew what tax to pay", "The emperor, so he could check the officials"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "That sounds like the inscription. The slips were working rules for officials.", "The rules affected farmers, but the slips were kept by an official, not handed out to farmers.", "The emperor set the rules, but these copies were kept by a local official doing the job."]
      explain: "They were made as working rules for officials. That is a different purpose from the inscription, which was for everyone to see."
```

## Practise: both questions

```step
stage: practise
insight: "Using context and purpose together on new cases, and correcting a purpose that is only content."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "The clay warriors were made for the First Emperor's tomb. No Qin text says why. Which is the best statement of their purpose?"
      options: ["Probably to guard and serve the emperor after his death", "To show soldiers in armour with bronze weapons", "Probably to show the Qin army to visitors to the tomb", "As practice pieces for craftsmen learning to work clay"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "That is what they show, which is content.", "They were buried in pits and covered over, so they were not made to be seen by visitors.", "Thousands of life-size, finished figures placed in a royal tomb were not practice pieces."]
      explain: "The tomb was built for the emperor. Most historians think the army was made to guard or serve him after death, reasoning from where it was placed and what it shows. That is an inference, not something a Qin source tells us."
  - check:
      type: question
      q: "Ravi says: 'The purpose of the inscription is that it shows the emperor.' What is the best reply?"
      options: ["That is what it shows. The purpose is why it was made", "That is right: what it shows is its purpose", "Nearly: its purpose is that it shows the emperor's laws", "Nearly: its purpose is that it is on a mountain"]
      answer: 0
      feedback: [null, "'Shows the emperor' says what is in it. That is content.", "Laws are still content: what it says. Purpose is what the maker wanted it to do.", "The mountain is where it was set up, which is origin. Purpose is why."]
      explain: "What a source shows is its content. Its purpose is what the maker wanted it to do."
```

```step

insight: "Writing a specific context and a purpose for a source of your own makes the questions yours."
check: { type: reflect, text: "In my own book I picked a source (from our unit, or one of Sources A to D) and wrote its context (what was going on, not just the place) and its purpose (why it was made). A partner read it and gave feedback on whether either was only a setting or only content." }
```

Write it in your own book or document, not on this page. Your partner or teacher reads it.

## Typical: what the purpose leaves out

```step
stage: make
tier: typical
insight: "A source made to persuade shows what its maker wants shown, so its purpose shapes what is left out."
check:
  type: question
  q: "Suppose a stone inscription was made to show the emperor's power and win support. Which is it least likely to include?"
  options: ["Signs that some people disliked his rule", "Praise for how he brought peace and order", "The new laws, weights and measures he set up", "The kingdoms he defeated to make his empire"]
  answer: 0
  feedback: [null, "That is just what it was made to include.", "It says he brought one set of laws, so this is included.", "Victories make a ruler look strong, so a source like this would happily name them."]
  explain: "A source made to win support is unlikely to show people who disagreed. Its purpose shapes what it leaves out."
```

## Wider: who was it written for?

```step
stage: make
tier: wider
insight: "Even a history can be shaped by who it was written for."
check:
  type: question
  q: "Sima Qian wrote his history for the Han court, about 100 years after the Qin had fallen. Which is the best point to make about this?"
  options: ["His readers belonged to the dynasty that replaced the Qin, which could shape what he chose to say", "A history written by a careful court historian can be taken as the whole truth", "He lived after the Qin, so he could not have known anything about them", "He wrote long after, so his history is a primary source for the Qin"]
  answer: 0
  feedback: [null, "Even careful histories are written by someone, for someone.", "He could use older records and stories. The point is who he was writing for.", "Written long after makes it secondary for the Qin, not primary."]
  explain: "Who a source was written for can shape it. That does not make it wrong, but it is worth asking."
```

Typical and wider steps are extras on the same idea. You do not need them to finish the lesson.

```teacher
learning: say what was going on when a source was made (context) and why it was
  probably made (purpose)
summary: "Students learn the next two questions to ask of any source: context
  (what was going on when it was made, not just the place) and purpose (why it
  was made). The second hinge lesson on this skill: students who answer 'ancient
  China' for context and 'it shows the emperor' for purpose cannot combine the
  four questions in the next lesson."
time: 40
timing: Predict and Try 8 min · Worked example 12 min · Vary 8 min · Practise 6
  min · Make 6 min. Typical and wider steps are extras and not counted in this.
goals:
  - I can say what was going on when a source was made, beyond its place and
    period.
  - I can say why a source was made, without mixing that up with what it shows.
  - I can write a context and a purpose for a source in my own words.
struggle: Students give a place or period for context ('ancient China') and
  content for purpose ('it shows the emperor'). Ask 'What was happening at that
  moment?' and 'What did the maker want?', and let them argue before you settle
  it.
before: >
  This is a hinge lesson. Lesson 4 (what can it tell us?) needs students to
  treat all four questions as distinct. If this lesson goes thinly, the combined
  conclusion will blur context with setting and purpose with content. Spend the
  time here.


  Context and purpose are sometimes opinions or inferences. For ancient sources,
  historians reason from what they know of the time. The cards give one
  defensible reading. If your class's depth study has a different view of why an
  inscription or a tomb was made, discuss it. Judge the reasoning, not whether
  it matches the card.


  The worked example is ancient China in the Qin and Han period, and it is a
  model: the same questions work on any society. For the tomb (Source A), the
  usual reading is that the army was made to protect or serve the emperor after
  his death; no Qin text states this, so the lesson says "probably" and
  "historians think". The same goes for the inscription's purpose (to show power
  and win support): it is an inference from its content and context, not
  something the stone says. Accept other well-reasoned purposes. Keep modern
  links factual: the site is a World Heritage site; avoid claims about China
  today.


  Everything beyond the described sources is made up (Ravi, Dev). Do not ask
  students about their families or beliefs.
running:
  - "Predict: ask for votes. 'Ancient China' sounds like a context. Ask what it
    would leave out."
  - "Try: the match has four different purposes for four sources. Ask students
    to say why the label is different from the other three."
  - "Worked example: let Nib's mistake sit before explaining it. Ask students
    what 'ancient China' leaves out."
  - "What the card tells you (board): Purpose is offered as a label, but no
    sentence states one. A student who labels 'It says he brought peace and
    order' or the praise line as purpose has read purpose off content (the
    lesson's planted slip). Ask: where on the card does it say why? The point is
    that purpose is worked out, so historians say 'probably'."
  - "Vary: ask who each source was written for. The answer changes between
    Source B and Source C."
  - "Make: read one or two out if students are happy to, without names."
stuck:
  - see: A student gives 'ancient China' as a context.
    ask: What was going on in ancient China at that moment? What had just happened?
    fix: Go back to Source C. The Qin had just joined rival kingdoms into one
      empire. A setting says where. A context says what was happening.
  - see: A student gives what a source shows as its purpose.
    ask: Is that what it shows, or why someone made it?
    fix: Purpose is what the maker wanted it to do. Showing the emperor is content.
  - see: A student says a source made to praise someone is useless.
    ask: Useless for what question?
    fix: It is good evidence of how the maker wanted to be seen. Lesson 4 picks this
      up.
stretch: Sima Qian wrote for the Han court, about a century after the Qin fell.
  Who his readers were could shape what he chose to say. Does that make his
  history wrong? This is the same idea at greater width. It does not go on to
  the next lesson.
support: "A card with two questions: 'What was going on? (an event or condition,
  not a place)' and 'What was it for? (what did the maker want?)'. Students
  write one sentence for each."
leads: >
  Next in Source origin and purpose: What can this source tell us? (all four
  questions together).


  Wider (teacher choice, not part of the student steps): ACARA's elaboration for
  AC9HH7S03 includes explaining "the difficulties in identifying the origin and
  purpose of some sources, such as the Kimberley Bradshaw paintings". These are
  culturally significant to First Nations people and are not used as an example
  here. If you use them, start from ACARA's elaboration and ask your school's
  First Nations contact for community-approved material.
exit:
  q: The First Emperor had an inscription cut into stone on a mountain. Give its
    context and its purpose, in a sentence each.
  a: "Context: the Qin had just defeated rival kingdoms and joined them into one
    empire. Purpose: probably to show his power and win people's support for his
    rule (accept other reasoned purposes)."
explain: >
  **Context** is what was going on when a source was made. A place or a period
  is not enough.


  **Purpose** is why it was made. What it shows is its content, not its purpose.
class:
  inquiry:
    q: Why would a ruler cut words into stone on a mountain? What was going on that
      made it worth the trouble?
    prompts:
      - Who was meant to read it?
      - What would the ruler want them to think?
    notes: Accept a range of answers if the reasoning is sound. Push for something
      specific that was happening, not a general reason.
  activities:
    - at: predict
      kind: activity
      title: Setting or context?
      minutes: 4
      do: >
        Read out pairs of statements about Source C (for example 'it was ancient
        China' and 'the Qin had just joined rival kingdoms'). Students say which
        is a setting and which is a context.
      notes: A setting says where and when. A context says what was happening. Do not
        settle it. Ask for the reason.
    - at: make
      kind: discussion
      title: What was it for?
      minutes: 4
      do: >
        Show Sources A to D. Ask pairs to give each one a purpose in six words
        or fewer. Compare.
      notes: Purposes will differ between sources made for the same ruler. That
        difference is the point.
  questions:
    - at: investigate
      title: Which is purpose?
      type: question
      q: Which of these is the likely purpose of the stone inscription?
      options:
        - Probably to show the emperor's power and win support
        - To show the emperor and the laws he made
        - To record that there was peace everywhere
        - To mark the place he stopped on his tour
      answer: 0
      explain: Purpose is why it was made. The second and third say what it shows or
        says (content). The fourth is about where it was set up (origin).
```
